analysis.one_liner: Makes expanded health insurance subsidies permanent and repeals Medicaid and Medicare cuts enacted by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
analysis.headline: The bill has 141 Democratic cosponsors but has sat in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote since its August 1 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make permanent the expanded premium tax credits that help people buy coverage on the health insurance marketplaces — those expanded credits are scheduled to end after 2025. It would also repeal health provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the 2025 reconciliation law, including new Medicaid eligibility and verification rules and a shorter window for retroactive Medicaid coverage. In short, it protects and expands subsidized health coverage, at a cost of ongoing federal spending.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy insurance through the marketplaces, especially the millions who rely on the expanded premium tax credits scheduled to lapse after 2025 — including households above the current 400%-of-poverty income cap, who would newly qualify. Medicaid enrollees also benefit: the bill repeals new eligibility and verification requirements and restores the longer window for retroactive Medicaid coverage. Hospitals and clinics benefit indirectly because fewer people lose coverage means less unpaid care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace insurance buyers and Medicaid enrollees

how_it_helps.text: It permanently eliminates the 400%-of-poverty income cap on premium tax credits, so households above that level can get help paying for marketplace coverage.
It lowers the sliding-scale percentages people pay for marketplace premiums across all income tiers, raising the size of the credit for eligible taxpayers.

It repeals health-related provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including certain Medicaid and Medicare eligibility and verification requirements, the reduced window for retroactive Medicaid coverage, and new premium tax credit verification requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through permanently higher federal spending on the premium tax credits with no income cap, and larger projected deficits. Some of the added subsidy under the expanded schedule goes to middle- and upper-income households that previously paid full price.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes any income cap on subsidy eligibility entirely, so the federal government would help pay premiums for households at every income level, with the wealthiest limited to paying 8.5% of income for benchmark coverage.
It makes what were designed as temporary, pandemic-era enhancements permanent, locking in long-term federal spending rather than a measured response to a temporary crisis.

It repeals the OBBBA's eligibility and income verification requirements for Medicaid and premium tax credits, which that law's supporters presented as safeguards against improper enrollment; removing them could increase improper payments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and large: letting the enhanced credits lapse at the end of 2025 would sharply raise premiums for people buying marketplace coverage, and the OBBBA provisions would add new documentation hurdles and a shorter retroactive-coverage window for Medicaid. The cost is that the bill answers that problem with the most expansive possible design — permanent, uncapped subsidies — rather than a temporary or income-limited extension, so a meaningful share of new federal spending goes to households that previously paid full price.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sits with the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees, which have taken no action on it since it was referred on August 1.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Gray introduced the bill on August 1, 2025, and it was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history after the referral.
All 141 cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans have signed on.
Under current law, the expanded premium tax credits apply only through 2025, so the underlying question — whether they lapse — remains unresolved while the bill awaits committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final winner yet. The status quo holds: the OBBBA health provisions remain law and the enhanced subsidies are still scheduled to expire after 2025, while the bill waits in committee without any scheduled action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Undecided; the bill waits in committee

for.name: Rep. Adam Gray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and the expanded premium tax credit and OBBBA repeal provisions.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Controls the House floor schedule and committee agendas
against.what_they_did: Have taken no action to schedule a markup or floor vote since the August 1 referral; the bill's action history ends there.

sides.party_line_note: All 141 cosponsors are House Democrats, none of the 223 House Republicans have signed on, and the bill awaits action under a Republican majority.

industries.note: Premium tax credits are paid through insurers, so permanently expanding them locks in a large base of subsidized marketplace customers and revenue even as insurers remain regulated. Ordinary people gain affordable coverage through the same private channel, so the industry's interest here runs alongside theirs.

Repealing the OBBBA's Medicaid eligibility and verification provisions and restoring the longer retroactive-coverage window would keep more people enrolled, reducing uncompensated care costs that otherwise get shifted onto providers and paying patients.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action two months after referral, and a House Republican majority, the bill is unlikely to advance on its own. Its realistic path runs indirectly: the enhanced premium tax credits are scheduled to expire after 2025, which could force a negotiated extension into a must-pass bill, though the OBBBA repeal provisions would be a much harder sell with the party that enacted them in control.
